lesson.title: Calling It: When a Result Counts as Statistically Significant
lesson.summary: A result is statistically significant when its p-value falls below the pre-chosen significance level, the formal rule that converts a p-value into a reject-or-not decision.
lesson.body:
The definition is a direct comparison of two numbers built up over the last two chapters: a result is called statistically significant when p-value is less than alpha. If p is less than alpha, reject H0, the result is statistically significant. If p is greater than or equal to alpha, fail to reject H0, the result is not statistically significant. There is no in-between category by design, the framework forces a binary decision even though the underlying evidence sits on a continuous scale.

Apply this to the cereal boxes, where p = 0.0456. At alpha = 0.05, since 0.0456 is less than 0.05, the result is statistically significant: reject H0: mu = 16, and conclude there is evidence the mean fill weight differs from 16 ounces. At alpha = 0.01, since 0.0456 is not less than 0.01, the result is not statistically significant at that stricter level: fail to reject H0, the evidence is not strong enough at that standard. This matches the critical value comparison from the previous chapter exactly, since z = negative 2.00 was beyond plus or minus 1.96 but not beyond plus or minus 2.576.

An important nuance: "not significant" is not the same as "H0 is proven true." It only means the collected evidence was not strong enough to overturn H0 at the chosen standard, and a different sample, a larger sample, or a different alpha could produce a different verdict. It is also worth separating two distinct ideas that get blurred in casual speech: "statistically significant" is a technical, binary label about whether p is less than alpha, which is a separate question from whether a result is practically or scientifically important. As noted when interpreting p-values, a large enough sample can make a tiny, practically trivial difference technically significant, so significance alone never settles whether a result actually matters.

Significance is the technical trigger for a decision, but writing a complete, correct conclusion in the context of the original problem is its own skill, and that is the subject of the next chapter.
